questions.stem: A 76 year old man has a 2 year history of slowly worsening breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. He smoked 30 pack years and was a bank manager. He takes no regular medicines. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. He has clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral basal reticular shadowing: lower zone fibrosis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gradual exertional breathlessness, dry cough, clubbing and fine bibasal crackles in an older ex-smoker with basal reticulation is IPF; asbestosis needs an exposure history.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
steps.x: Elderly ex-smoking man, gradual dyspnoea, dry cough, clubbing, velcro crackles, basal reticulation.

elim: Similar basal fibrosis, but he has no asbestos exposure and no pleural plaques.
Does not cause clubbing or fine velcro crackles.
Crackles but no clubbing; would expect oedema and orthopnoea.
Younger patients, upper zone change and hilar nodes.

steps.x: D: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. IPF is the most common fibrotic lung disease; median age 70, men and smokers.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. She started a weekly oral disease-modifying drug 14 months ago with folic acid. Over 3 months she has developed a dry cough and breathlessness walking her dog. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There are fine crackles at both bases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her lung disease?
questions.e: A weekly DMARD given with folic acid is methotrexate, which causes pneumonitis and lower lobe fibrosis; the other drugs are not typical causes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her lung disease?
Weekly DMARD with folic acid = methotrexate; new dry cough and basal crackles.

elim: A biologic given by injection, not a weekly oral drug with folic acid.
Causes hypertension and nephrotoxicity, not typically pulmonary fibrosis.
Causes retinal toxicity, not lung fibrosis.
Taken daily, not weekly with folic acid; lung toxicity is rare.

steps.x: D: Methotrexate. Methotrexate is a classic drug cause of pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and has taken amiodarone for 2 years. He has 4 months of progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. His skin has a slate-grey tinge in sun-exposed areas. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 64 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. He has fine bibasal crackles.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Amiodarone causes pulmonary fibrosis (and slate-grey skin); always ask about drugs in new fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Long-term amiodarone (with skin pigmentation) plus new basal fibrosis.

elim: Gives copious purulent sputum and coarse crackles.
Possible with AF, but the grey skin and long amiodarone course point to drug toxicity.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or mass; the crackles are bilateral and fine.
Sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain, not 4 months of dry cough with crackles.

steps.x: A: Amiodarone-induced pulmonary fibrosis. Amiodarone causes lower lobe pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has had seropositive rheumatoid arthritis for 12 years, treated with hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine. She has 8 months of breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. She has swan-neck deformities of her fingers and fine bibasal crackles. HRCT shows reticulation in both lower lobes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: RA is a secondary cause of lower lobe interstitial fibrosis; she does not take methotrexate, and bronchiectasis would give purulent sputum.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Autoimmune disease + basal fibrosis + no culprit drug.

elim: Also linked with RA, but gives purulent sputum, coarse crackles and dilated bronchi.
She does not take methotrexate.
Would give dullness and reduced breath sounds, not reticulation.
Upper zone change and hilar nodes, not basal reticulation with RA.

steps.x: C: Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease. Autoimmune disease (e.g. RA) is a cause of lower lobe fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has slowly worsening breathlessness over 3 years. He was a pipe lagger in a shipyard from 1965 to 1985. He has clubbing and fine bibasal end-inspiratory crackles. Chest X-ray shows basal reticular shadowing and calcified pleural plaques on both hemidiaphragms. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.84 with FVC 61% predicted.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his lung fibrosis?
questions.e: Asbestosis is a secondary cause of lower lobe fibrosis; pleural plaques confirm asbestos exposure and separate it from IPF.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his lung fibrosis?
Asbestos job + pleural plaques + lower lobe fibrosis.

elim: Upper lobe disease in coal miners, without pleural plaques.
Organic antigen exposure and upper lobe fibrosis.
Looks similar, but pleural plaques and lagging point to asbestos.
Upper lobe nodular fibrosis in quarry workers and sandblasters.

steps.x: A: Asbestosis. Asbestosis causes lower lobe fibrosis; pleural plaques mark asbestos exposure.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has worked for 35 years as a stonemason cutting granite and sandstone. He has 2 years of breathlessness and a dry cough. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources). It also shows eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his lung fibrosis?
questions.e: Silicosis gives upper zone nodular fibrosis with eggshell hilar calcification; asbestosis, IPF, RA and drugs cause lower lobe fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his lung fibrosis?

clues: eggshell calcification of the hilar nodes
steps.x: Silica job + upper zone fibrosis + eggshell nodes.

elim: Lower lobe fibrosis with pleural plaques.
Basal, not upper zone, fibrosis.
No methotrexate; drug fibrosis is lower lobe.
No joint disease, and RA fibrosis is basal.

steps.x: E: Silicosis. Upper lobe fibrosis: CHARTS (Coal, Histiocytosis/HP, Ankylosing spondylitis, Radiation, TB, Silicosis/Sarcoidosis).

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman had Hodgkin lymphoma treated with chemotherapy and mantle field irradiation 20 years ago. She has had slowly increasing breathlessness for 3 years. She has never smoked and has no occupational exposures. Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper zone fibrotic shadowing with paramediastinal volume loss.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her fibrosis?
questions.e: Radiation fibrosis follows the treatment field (here mantle field, upper and paramediastinal); it is one of the CHARTS upper lobe causes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her fibrosis?
Upper lobe fibrosis in the old radiation field.

elim: No exposure, and asbestosis affects the lower lobes.
Basal predominant and usually in older men.
No nitrofurantoin; drug fibrosis is lower lobe.
Gives lower lobe fibrosis with Raynaud's and skin thickening.

steps.x: D: Previous radiotherapy. R in CHARTS = radiation: previous radiotherapy causes upper lobe fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 2 years of Raynaud's phenomenon, tight shiny skin on her fingers and difficulty swallowing. She now has breathlessness on exertion and a dry cough. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. There are fine bibasal crackles. HRCT shows ground-glass change and reticulation in both lower lobes.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune cause of lower lobe fibrosis; ankylosing spondylitis, TB and sarcoidosis are upper lobe (CHARTS).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: tight shiny skin on her fingers
steps.x: Scleroderma features + lower lobe fibrosis.

elim: Causes upper lobe fibrosis in men with back pain.
Needs an antigen exposure and gives upper lobe change when chronic.
Upper lobe disease with fever and weight loss.
Hilar nodes and upper zone change, not sclerodactyly.

steps.x: E: Systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease. Lower lobe causes: RA, IPF, asbestosis, SLE, scleroderma and drugs.

questions.stem: A 43 year old man keeps a large aviary of budgerigars. Over the last month he has had three episodes of fever, aching muscles, a dry cough and breathlessness, each starting 4 to 6 hours after cleaning out the cages and settling in a day or two. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hazy airspace opacification.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent fever, myalgia and dyspnoea 4 to 6 hours after bird exposure with bilateral airspace change is acute EAA (bird fancier's lung); psittacosis would not recur with each exposure.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: 4 to 6 hours after cleaning out the cages
steps.x: Fever, myalgia and dry cough hours after organic antigen exposure, recurring.

elim: Wheeze within minutes of exposure, not fever and myalgia hours later.
Would not recur each time he cleans the cages and settle in a day.
Chronic and progressive, not episodic fever.
Bird-related infection, but would not recur and resolve with each exposure.

steps.x: B: Acute extrinsic allergic alveolitis. Acute EAA: fever, myalgia, dry cough, dyspnoea and bilateral airspace opacification after exposure.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has farmed cattle for 45 years and has forked damp, mouldy hay every winter. He has had several feverish episodes after hay work in the past. He now has 3 years of slowly progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. His oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. HRCT is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on HRCT?
o: Dilated bronchi larger than the adjacent arteries
questions.e: Chronic extrinsic allergic alveolitis (farmer's lung) leaves upper-lobe-predominant fibrosis; basal honeycombing alone suggests IPF.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on HRCT?

clues: forked damp, mouldy hay every winter
steps.x: Repeated farmer's lung episodes progressing to chronic disease.

elim: The typical IPF pattern; chronic EAA is upper lobe.
Classic for sarcoidosis.
Mark asbestos exposure.
The signet ring sign of bronchiectasis.

steps.x: E: Upper lobe predominant fibrosis. Chronic EAA causes upper-lobe-predominant fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman has 18 months of gradually increasing breathlessness and a dry cough with fatigue. HRCT has shown basal subpleural reticulation. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Her lips look slightly blue.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her hands?
o: Tar staining with a fine tremor
questions.e: Clubbing is common in IPF and other fibrotic lung disease, along with cyanosis and velcro crackles; the other signs belong to other conditions.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her hands?

clues: gradually increasing breathlessness and a dry cough
steps.x: Fibrotic lung disease with cyanosis.

elim: Osteoarthritis of the DIP joints; unrelated to lung fibrosis.
Painless palmar lesions of infective endocarditis.
White nails of hypoalbuminaemia.
Tar staining suggests smoking, and a fine tremor suggests salbutamol use or thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: A: Finger clubbing. Fibrotic lung disease: dry cough, SOB, fatigue, cyanosis, clubbing, velcro crackles.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with advanced idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has developed swollen ankles over 6 weeks. His pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. His JVP is raised by 6 cm, there is a loud P2 and pitting oedema to the knees. An echocardiogram is arranged.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
o: Dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 25%
Dilated right ventricle with raised pulmonary artery pressure
questions.e: Chronic hypoxaemia causes pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale; echo shows a dilated RV with raised PA pressure. Loud P2 and raised JVP are right-sided signs.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on echocardiography?
Hypoxic fibrotic lung disease with right heart failure signs.

elim: Left heart failure; his signs are right-sided with loud P2.
Would give muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus.
Infective endocarditis; no fever or murmur.
Gives an ejection systolic murmur and syncope, not right heart failure.

steps.x: B: Dilated right ventricle with raised pulmonary artery pressure. Advanced fibrosis causes pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale; echo assesses right heart strain.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man has just been diagnosed with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. He worked as an office clerk all his life. He smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 40 years. He has no pets and takes only atorvastatin. He has no joint or skin symptoms.
questions.q: Which feature of his history is the most important risk factor for his condition?
questions.e: Smoking is a major risk factor for IPF, which is commoner in older men; office work, statins and lack of pets are not risks.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of his history is the most important risk factor for his condition?
50 pack years in an older man.

elim: Statins are not a recognised cause of IPF.
Not an occupational exposure linked to fibrosis.
Lack of pets is protective against EAA, not a risk factor.
Avoids drug-induced fibrosis rather than causing it.

steps.x: B: Cigarette smoking. IPF is more common in men and smokers; smoking is a cause of fibrotic lung disease.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman has just been told she has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis after HRCT showed basal subpleural honeycombing. She is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines. Her FVC is 72% predicted. She asks her consultant what to expect without a lung transplant.
questions.q: Which best describes the prognosis of her condition?
o: Complete recovery with oral steroids in most patients
Normal life expectancy with no progression
Progressive disease with a median survival of about 3 to 5 years
questions.e: IPF is progressive and irreversible with a poor prognosis (median survival about 3 to 5 years); antifibrotics only slow decline.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the prognosis of her condition?
Established IPF with honeycombing.

elim: Steroids do not help IPF and may harm.
IPF is progressive with a poor prognosis.
Stopping smoking helps but does not reverse fibrosis.
Seen in Löfgren's sarcoidosis, not IPF.

steps.x: C: Progressive disease with a median survival of about 3 to 5 years. IPF is the commonest fibrotic lung disease and has a poor prognosis.

questions.stem: A 45 year old Black British woman had erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy 15 years ago. She now has 2 years of breathlessness and a dry cough. Her serum ACE is raised. Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper zone fibrosis with loss of volume and no hilar nodes. She has no occupational exposures.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her fibrosis?
questions.e: Previous sarcoidosis with raised ACE progressing to upper zone fibrosis (stage 4); the other options cause lower lobe fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her fibrosis?

clues: erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy 15 years ago
steps.x: Previous Löfgren picture, raised ACE, upper zone fibrosis.

elim: No exposure, and asbestosis is basal.
Basal, older men, and serum ACE would not be raised.
No joint disease; RA fibrosis is basal.
Causes lower lobe fibrosis.

steps.x: D: Sarcoidosis. S in CHARTS = sarcoidosis (and silicosis): upper lobe fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man has 14 months of progressive breathlessness and a dry cough. He has clubbing and fine bibasal crackles. His GP's chest X-ray shows bilateral reticular shadowing at the bases. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.83. He is referred to the respiratory clinic.
questions.q: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis and define its pattern?
questions.e: HRCT is the gold standard in fibrotic lung disease, showing the extent and pattern (e.g. UIP with honeycombing); biopsy is only for uncertain cases.

steps.x: The question asks: Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis and define its pattern?

clues: bilateral reticular shadowing at the bases
steps.x: Suspected fibrosis on X-ray and spirometry: now characterise it.

elim: Invasive and not first; HRCT usually makes the diagnosis.
Looks for pulmonary emboli, not interstitial pattern.
Assesses cor pulmonale, not the lung pattern.
Support EAA if suspected, but do not define the pattern.

steps.x: D: High-resolution CT chest. HRCT is the gold standard; it categorises the extent and pattern of fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has progressive exertional breathlessness and clubbing. HRCT shows clustered cystic airspaces with thick walls in the subpleural regions of both lower lobes, with traction bronchiectasis and minimal ground-glass change. The upper lobes are spared.
questions.q: Which is the most likely HRCT pattern?
questions.e: Basal subpleural honeycombing is a typical UIP pattern, the HRCT picture of IPF; without honeycombing it would be probable UIP.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely HRCT pattern?

clues: clustered cystic airspaces with thick walls
subpleural regions of both lower lobes
steps.x: Basal subpleural honeycombing.

elim: Used when change is variable or diffuse, not basal honeycombing.
Patchy consolidation, not honeycombing.
Basal reticulation without honeycombing; this scan has honeycombing.
Suggests a CHARTS cause; the upper lobes are spared here.

steps.x: D: Typical usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). Typical UIP = honeycombing, basal; probable UIP = no honeycombing; indeterminate = variable or diffuse.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has progressive breathlessness and fine bibasal crackles. HRCT shows reticulation with traction bronchiectasis in the subpleural bases of both lungs. No honeycombing is seen anywhere. There is no upper lobe predominance and no features to suggest another diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely HRCT classification?
questions.e: Basal subpleural reticulation with traction bronchiectasis but no honeycombing is probable UIP; typical UIP requires honeycombing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely HRCT classification?

clues: traction bronchiectasis in the subpleural bases
steps.x: Basal fibrosis but no honeycombing.

elim: Upper and mid zone predominant with air trapping.
Used when change is variable or diffuse rather than basal.
There is reticulation and traction bronchiectasis.
Requires honeycombing, which is absent.

steps.x: D: Probable UIP. Probable UIP = basal fibrosis without honeycombing.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 6 months of breathlessness and a dry cough. HRCT shows diffuse ground-glass change and reticulation in all zones, reported as indeterminate for UIP. He keeps chickens and takes no regular medicines. His autoimmune screen is negative. The multidisciplinary team cannot reach a diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: When HRCT is indeterminate, bronchoscopy with BAL helps (e.g. lymphocytosis suggests hypersensitivity pneumonitis); a repeat scan adds nothing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Uncertain HRCT pattern despite work-up.

elim: Less detailed than the HRCT he has already had.
Assesses right heart strain, not the cause of the lung disease.
Will not add information in such a short time.
He has a dry cough; this will not clarify the interstitial pattern.

steps.x: A: Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage. Uncertain cases may need bronchoscopy with BAL.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man with suspected idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has full lung function tests. He is an ex-smoker with clubbing and fine bibasal crackles, and his oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air. Spirometry shows FEV1 66% predicted and FVC 63% predicted, with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.84.

visual.title: FEV1/FVC ratio
visual.label: His ratio 0.84
visual.caption: Ratio above 0.7 with both volumes below 80%: restrictive.

questions.q: Which other result is most likely?
o: Normal total lung capacity and normal TLCO
Raised total lung capacity and raised TLCO
Raised total lung capacity and reduced TLCO
Reduced total lung capacity and raised TLCO
Reduced total lung capacity and reduced TLCO
questions.e: Fibrosis gives a restrictive defect with reduced TLC and VC and reduced TLCO from the thickened interstitium; raised TLC with low TLCO is emphysema.

steps.x: The question asks: Which other result is most likely?
Restrictive spirometry: both FEV1 and FVC below 80%, ratio above 0.7.

elim: Fibrosis reduces both lung volumes and gas transfer.
Not seen in fibrosis; raised TLCO suggests haemorrhage or polycythaemia.
Raised TLC with low TLCO is emphysema.
TLCO is reduced in fibrosis because of thickened alveolar walls.

steps.x: E: Reduced total lung capacity and reduced TLCO. Restrictive pattern: low VC and TLC with reduced TLCO.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has 5 months of breathlessness and a dry cough. She has early morning stiffness and swelling of the small joints of her hands, and dry eyes. HRCT shows basal interstitial fibrosis. She takes no medicines and has no occupational exposures. Her FBC and renal function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Autoimmune screen including rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP and ANA
questions.e: New ILD with inflammatory arthritis and sicca needs an autoimmune screen to find a treatable connective tissue cause.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Fibrosis with clues to connective tissue disease.

elim: Reserved for uncertain cases after non-invasive tests.
A marker for sarcoidosis, which gives hilar nodes and upper lobe change.
For EAA, but she has no antigen exposure.
TB is unlikely with basal fibrosis and no systemic features.

steps.x: A: Autoimmune screen including rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP and ANA. Work-up includes an autoimmune screen and routine bloods.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man works in a mushroom farm. He has recurrent episodes of fever, myalgia and breathlessness several hours after work, with bilateral airspace shadowing on chest X-ray during attacks. His symptoms settle on days off.
questions.q: Which blood test would best support the diagnosis?
o: Serum precipitins to fungal and mould antigens
questions.e: Serum precipitins (IgG antibodies) to the relevant fungal or mould antigen support EAA, a type III reaction; IgE is for type I allergy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which blood test would best support the diagnosis?
Organic antigen, delayed systemic reaction: suspected EAA.

elim: For rheumatoid arthritis.
For bacteraemia; attacks settle without antibiotics.
Raised in sarcoidosis.
Raised in atopy and ABPA; EAA is type III, not IgE-mediated.

steps.x: D: Serum precipitins to fungal and mould antigens. EAA is confirmed with serum precipitins (IgG) to Aspergillus and mould antigens.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has persistent atrial fibrillation and has failed rate control. His cardiologist plans to start amiodarone. He has no breathing symptoms and his chest is clear. He smoked for 20 years and stopped 10 years ago.
questions.q: Which investigation should be done before starting the drug?
questions.e: A baseline chest X-ray (with LFTs and TFTs) is done before amiodarone to detect pre-existing lung disease and allow later comparison.

steps.x: The question asks: Which investigation should be done before starting the drug?
Baseline before a drug known to cause pulmonary fibrosis.

elim: Invasive and not needed in an asymptomatic patient.
Looks for pulmonary emboli; not a screening test.
Not routine for screening; a baseline chest X-ray is used.
Not relevant to drug lung toxicity.

steps.x: B: Chest X-ray. Amiodarone should prompt a chest X-ray before starting, to check for pre-existing lung disease.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis confirmed by a multidisciplinary team. His FVC is 68% predicted and has fallen by 8% in a year. He has started pulmonary rehabilitation. He has no liver disease and takes no anticoagulants.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to slow disease progression?
questions.e: Pirfenidone and nintedanib are the first-line disease-modifying drugs in IPF and slow FVC decline; steroids and azathioprine are harmful.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate drug to slow disease progression?
Confirmed, progressing IPF in an eligible patient.

elim: Immunosuppression is harmful in IPF.
Can itself cause pulmonary fibrosis.
Sometimes used in a subset, but it is not the first-line disease-modifying drug.
Steroids do not help IPF and increase harm.

steps.x: C: Nintedanib. First-line antifibrotics: pirfenidone or nintedanib, which slow progression.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has taken amiodarone for 3 years for ventricular tachycardia. He has 3 months of breathlessness and a dry cough. HRCT shows new bilateral lower lobe interstitial fibrosis. His cardiologist agrees an alternative rhythm treatment is possible. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: In drug-induced fibrosis, stop the drug (steroids may then help); antifibrotics are for IPF.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

clues: new bilateral lower lobe interstitial fibrosis
steps.x: Drug-induced fibrosis with a safe alternative.

elim: Antifibrotics are for IPF; the cause must be removed.
Toxicity is dose-related; this will worsen it.
Helpful later but does not remove the cause.
Premature before removing the cause.

steps.x: E: Stop amiodarone. Treat the underlying cause: remove the exposure or stop the drug.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is reviewed in clinic. She stopped smoking 10 years ago. Her resting oxygen saturation is 87% breathing air on two visits 3 weeks apart. She has no hypercapnia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: No change, as oxygen does not help fibrosis
questions.e: Persistent resting hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 7.3 kPa) in a non-smoker is an indication for LTOT in fibrotic lung disease; NIV is for hypercapnia.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Persistent resting hypoxaemia, stable, non-smoker.

elim: Used for hypercapnic respiratory failure, which she does not have.
Fibrosis is not an airflow obstruction problem.
She meets criteria; oxygen corrects her hypoxaemia.
Does not help IPF.

steps.x: B: Long-term oxygen therapy. Supportive care includes long-term oxygen if hypoxic.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Despite nintedanib and pulmonary rehabilitation his FVC has fallen steadily (see item resources). He is otherwise fit, has a BMI of 25 and stopped smoking 12 years ago. He has no other significant illnesses.

visual.title: FVC % predicted
visual.caption: Steady fall in FVC despite antifibrotic treatment.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: A young, fit patient progressing despite antifibrotics should be referred for lung transplant assessment; steroids and azathioprine are harmful.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Progressing on treatment, young and fit.

elim: Immunosuppression is harmful in IPF.
Steroids do not slow IPF.
Removes the only disease-modifying treatment without a plan.
He is young and fit enough to be considered for transplant.

steps.x: C: Refer for lung transplant assessment. Lung transplantation may be considered in a subset with severe or refractory disease.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man has end-stage idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and is not a transplant candidate. He already uses long-term oxygen with an ambulatory supply. He remains breathless at rest and is distressed by it. He wants to stay at home and focus on comfort.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment for his breathlessness?
questions.e: In end-stage fibrosis, after oxygen, low-dose opiates (or benzodiazepines for anxiety) relieve breathlessness; transplant is not an option for him.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment for his breathlessness?
End-stage disease already on oxygen; comfort-focused.

elim: Does not help IPF and causes harm.
For fluid overload, not fibrotic breathlessness.
He is not a candidate.
A mucolytic for bronchiectasis.

steps.x: C: Low-dose oral morphine. End-stage: LTOT plus ambulatory oxygen first; then low-dose opiates or benzodiazepines.

questions.stem: A 73 year old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis rings her GP. Over 5 days she has become breathless walking across a room, when last month she could walk to the shops. Her oxygen saturation measured at home is 83% breathing air, from a usual 94%. She has no chest pain.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase her inhaler and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Rapidly worsening breathlessness and hypoxia in fibrotic lung disease (acute exacerbation, infection or PE) needs urgent hospital assessment.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Rapid deterioration with new hypoxia.

elim: Inhalers do not treat fibrosis, and the delay is unsafe.
Too slow for acute deterioration with hypoxia.
Needs assessment for the cause first.
Needs assessment first; causes include infection or PE.

steps.x: C: Same-day hospital assessment. Worsening breathlessness and hypoxia suggest progressing disease and need urgent assessment.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man sees his GP with 9 months of exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. He has clubbing and fine bibasal crackles. Chest X-ray shows basal reticular shadowing and spirometry is restrictive. He has no exposures and takes no drugs.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Prescribe a salbutamol inhaler and review in 3 months
questions.e: Suspected IPF needs referral to a respiratory specialist for HRCT and MDT diagnosis; steroids and inhalers do not help.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Suspected fibrotic lung disease in primary care.

elim: Inhalers do not treat fibrosis and delay diagnosis.
Delays diagnosis of a progressive disease.
No infection is described.
Steroids do not help IPF and the diagnosis is not yet made.

steps.x: B: Refer to a respiratory specialist. Refer to a respiratory specialist for HRCT, MDT diagnosis, antifibrotics and rehab.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis takes pirfenidone. Her resting oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air. She has lost confidence and walks less because she gets breathless, and she has lost 4 kg. She feels low about her diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Pulmonary rehabilitation with dietetic and psychological support
questions.e: Pulmonary rehabilitation with dietary and psychological support improves exercise tolerance and quality of life; she is not hypoxic, so LTOT is not indicated.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Deconditioning, weight loss and low mood; not hypoxic.

elim: The two antifibrotics are not combined.
She is not hypoxic at rest.
Does not help IPF.
Not the next step for her symptoms of deconditioning and low mood.

steps.x: D: Pulmonary rehabilitation with dietetic and psychological support. Supportive care: pulmonary rehab, LTOT if hypoxic, dietary advice and psychological support.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man has idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. A lung biopsy shows patchy areas of dense collagen next to normal lung, with clusters of actively proliferating fibroblasts (fibroblastic foci) beneath damaged alveolar epithelium. There is little inflammation.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his disease?
o: Granulomatous inflammation from an unknown antigen
Immune complex deposition from inhaled organic antigen
Permanent dilation of bronchi from infection
Repeated alveolar epithelial injury with aberrant wound healing
questions.e: IPF results from repeated alveolar epithelial injury with aberrant wound healing, so fibroblasts deposit excess collagen and ECM that replaces normal lung.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his disease?
Fibroblast foci beneath injured epithelium with little inflammation.

elim: That is sarcoidosis.
That is extrinsic allergic alveolitis.
That is bronchiectasis.
That is emphysema.

steps.x: E: Repeated alveolar epithelial injury with aberrant wound healing. IPF: repeated epithelial injury and aberrant healing; fibroblasts lay down excess collagen.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis has spirometry showing FEV1 1.5 L (65% predicted) and FVC 1.75 L (62% predicted), giving an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.86. Her medical student asks why the ratio is normal when both values are low.
questions.q: Which best explains the preserved FEV1/FVC ratio?
o: Both volumes fall proportionately because the lungs are stiff but the airways are open
Bronchoconstriction lowers FEV1 more than FVC
Loss of elastic recoil from emphysema
Mucus plugging of the small airways
questions.e: Stiff, fibrotic lungs cannot expand, so FVC and FEV1 fall together and the ratio stays above 0.7 (often raised by increased radial traction on airways).

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the preserved FEV1/FVC ratio?
Restrictive: small, stiff lungs with normal airways.

elim: Air trapping lowers FVC and occurs in obstruction.
That gives a low ratio (obstruction).
Causes obstruction with a low ratio.
Causes obstruction, as in bronchiectasis.

steps.x: B: Both volumes fall proportionately because the lungs are stiff but the airways are open. Fibrosis reduces compliance, so both FEV1 and FVC fall; the ratio is preserved or raised.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has had idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis for 6 years. He has clubbing, fine bibasal crackles and an oxygen saturation of 89% breathing air. His latest HRCT shows extensive basal honeycombing, which was not present at diagnosis.
questions.q: Which best describes what the honeycombing represents?
o: Cystic airspaces with thick fibrotic walls replacing normal alveoli
Enlarged airspaces from alveolar wall destruction without fibrosis
Reversible inflammation of the alveolar walls
questions.e: Honeycombing represents end-stage fibrosis, where cystic airspaces with thick fibrotic walls replace normal alveolar architecture; it is irreversible.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes what the honeycombing represents?
New honeycombing after years of disease.

elim: Describes bronchiectasis.
Describes emphysema.
Describes oedema or consolidation.
Ground glass can be inflammatory, but honeycombing is irreversible.

steps.x: A: Cystic airspaces with thick fibrotic walls replacing normal alveoli. Honeycombing is end-stage fibrosis: cystic airspaces bound by thick fibrotic walls.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man is receiving bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin for a testicular germ cell tumour. After the third cycle he develops a dry cough and breathlessness, with fine bibasal crackles and a fall in TLCO.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lung injury?
o: Direct cytotoxic injury to alveolar epithelial cells
Granuloma formation from an unknown antigen
questions.e: Bleomycin causes direct cytotoxic (free radical) injury to alveolar epithelial cells, leading to fibrosis; it is dose-related.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his lung injury?
Bleomycin plus new fibrosis.

elim: Would cause fever and consolidation; fibrosis with a falling TLCO points to drug toxicity.
That is sarcoidosis.
Gives wheeze and obstruction, not fibrosis.
Would cause sudden breathlessness with clear lungs.

steps.x: B: Direct cytotoxic injury to alveolar epithelial cells. Drug fibrosis: direct cytotoxic injury to alveolar epithelium and/or immune-mediated hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman started nitrofurantoin for a urinary tract infection 6 days ago. She now has fever, a dry cough, breathlessness and a rash. Her eosinophil count is 1.9 × 10⁹/L. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial shadowing. She has never had lung problems.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her lung reaction?
o: Bacterial pneumonia from the urinary organism
questions.e: Acute nitrofurantoin lung (fever, rash, eosinophilia within days) is an immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction; chronic use causes cytotoxic fibrosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her lung reaction?
Acute reaction days after starting, with rash and eosinophilia.

elim: Would not explain a rash and eosinophilia.
Occurs after months to years of use, not 6 days.
No cardiac history; eosinophilia and rash suggest hypersensitivity.
Does not cause eosinophilia and rash.

steps.x: D: Immune-mediated hypersensitivity reaction. Drug lung disease can be immune-mediated hypersensitivity as well as cytotoxic.

questions.stem: A 50 year old dairy farmer has recurrent fever, myalgia and breathlessness starting 5 hours after handling mouldy hay. His oxygen saturation is 92% breathing air during an attack. Serum precipitins against Saccharopolyspora rectivirgula are positive. Biopsy shows loosely formed granulomas and lymphocytic alveolitis.
questions.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is mainly responsible?
questions.e: EAA (farmer's lung) is a type III, immune complex reaction to inhaled organic antigen, shown by precipitating IgG antibodies; type I gives immediate wheeze.

steps.x: The question asks: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is mainly responsible?
Delayed by hours with precipitating IgG antibodies.

elim: Causes immediate wheeze within minutes, as in asthma.
As in Goodpasture's, not inhaled antigen.
Contributes to granulomas, but immune complexes with precipitins are the main reaction.
As in Graves' disease.

steps.x: C: Type III (immune complex). Extrinsic allergic alveolitis is a type III hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.stem: A 75 year old man with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is breathless when he walks. His total lung capacity is 58% predicted. His chest wall and diaphragm are normal and he is not obese. A student asks why his lung volumes are so small.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Air trapping from small airway collapse
Loss of alveolar walls increasing compliance
Shunting of blood through consolidated lung
Thickened, stiff interstitium reducing lung compliance
questions.e: Collagen-filled, thickened interstitium reduces compliance so the lungs cannot inflate; emphysema increases compliance and volumes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely explanation?

clues: chest wall and diaphragm are normal
steps.x: Small lungs with a normal chest wall: the lungs themselves are stiff.

elim: Raises lung volumes, as in COPD.
That is emphysema, with large lungs.
His diaphragm and chest wall are normal.
Explains hypoxia, not small volumes.

steps.x: E: Thickened, stiff interstitium reducing lung compliance. Fibrosis reduces lung compliance, giving a restrictive pattern.
